findings.issue: Source simile opens 'As when there is a heavy swell upon the sea'; candidate turns it into an imperative 'Think of a heavy swell on the sea when the waves are dumb', which is an added device and breaks the 'as when... so' form.
findings.fix: He took the shield of his son Thrasymedes from the tent, where it lay gleaming with bronze, since Thrasymedes had taken his father’s shield. He also picked up his redoubtable bronze-shod spear. As soon as he was outside he saw the disastrous rout of the Achaeans. Their wall was overthrown, and they were fleeing in confusion before the Trojans. As when there is a heavy swell on the sea and the waves are dumb, they watch for the quarter from which the fierce winds may spring on them, but they stay where they are and roll neither this way nor that, until some particular wind sweeps down from heaven to decide for them. In the same way the old man was torn over whether to make for the crowd of Danaans or go in search of Agamemnon. In the end he thought it best to go to the son of Atreus. Meanwhile the armies kept fighting and killing one another, and the hard bronze rattled on their bodies as they thrust at each other with swords and spears.

findings.issue: Zeus's question 'What do you want that you have come hither from Olympus' lost the clause 'What do you want'; candidate has only 'Why have you come here from Olympus'.
findings.fix: Hera did as he asked. She swore the oath and called on all the gods of the nether world, the ones called Titans, as witnesses. When the oath was complete, the two wrapped themselves in a thick mist and hurried on, leaving Lemnos and Imbrus behind them. Soon they came to many-fountained Ida, mother of wild beasts, and to Lectum, where they left the sea and went on over land. The tops of the forest trees rustled beneath their feet. Sleep stopped here. Before Zeus could catch sight of him, he climbed a lofty pine—the tallest that lifted its head toward heaven on all Ida. He hid among the branches and sat there looking like the sweet-singing bird of the mountains, which the gods call Chalcis and men call Cymindis. Hera then went on to Gargarus, the topmost peak of Ida, and Zeus, driver of the clouds, saw her. The moment he did, he was filled with the same passionate desire for her that he had felt when they first enjoyed each other’s embraces and slept together without their dear parents knowing anything about it. He went up to her and said, “What do you want, that you have come here from Olympus, and with no chariot or horses to carry you?”

findings.issue: 'The son of Tydeus, Odysseus and Agamemnon' without a comma after Odysseus reads as if Odysseus were the son of Tydeus (three persons intended).
findings.fix: So he spoke, and they did as he said. The son of Tydeus, Odysseus, and Agamemnon, wounded though they were, put the others in order and went everywhere arranging the exchanges of armor. The most valiant took the best armor and gave the worse to the worse man. When they had put on their bronze armor, they marched on with Poseidon at their head. In his strong hand he gripped his terrible sword, sharp of edge and flashing like lightning. Woe to anyone who meets it in the day of battle; all men shake with fear and keep away from it.

findings.issue: Butler's text is garbled ('through the tops of when it is blowing its hardest', a word such as 'trees' or 'oaks' missing); candidate's 'through the treetops' is a sensible reading.
